answers.children: Yes — Newfoundlands are exceptionally good with children thanks to their gentle nature and immense patience. Their giant build and calm temperament allow them to tolerate ear tugs and tail pulls from toddlers without reaction, and their protective loyalty means they often position themselves as quiet guardians during play. Bred for water rescue, their strength translates into careful movement around small family members. (PawLabs child-friendly score: 9/10)
answers.other-pets: Yes — Newfoundlands generally get along with other pets because of their sociable and gentle temperament. Their low prey drive and patient personality reduce tension with household animals, though their massive size can accidentally overwhelm smaller companions during calm interactions. The protective instinct that once served them in rescue work extends to living peacefully alongside other dogs and cats.
answers.exercise: Newfoundlands need around one hour of moderate exercise daily, such as a leisurely walk or a swim. Without this their calm energy can lead to restlessness and destructive behaviour indoors. Their history of water rescue and draft work makes swimming their preferred activity, as the breed thrives in cool water that suits its heavy build and thick coat rather than intense running.
answers.shedding: Yes — Newfoundlands shed heavily year-round with seasonal spikes. Their medium-length double coat is dense and water-repellent, producing large amounts of loose undercoat that forms tumbleweeds across floors and clings to furniture. The outer guard hairs and soft undercoat require regular removal to prevent matting, especially on the chest and behind the legs where the fur is thickest.
answers.hypoallergenic: Newfoundlands are not hypoallergenic; their medium double coat sheds heavily and spreads loose hair and dander throughout the house. The thick, water-repellent outer layer traps debris from their working days in icy waters, demanding frequent cleaning. No breed is genuinely hypoallergenic and Newfoundlands are rarely suggested to allergy sufferers.
answers.training: Newfoundlands are moderately easy to train because of their intelligence and willingness to please. Their gentle loyalty and protective instinct make them responsive to consistent guidance, though their giant size and independent streak from draft work can slow progress if sessions lack clear direction. The breed’s calm energy rewards patient handlers who channel its strength into useful tasks.
answers.lifespan: Newfoundlands live 9-11 years. Their giant build and heavy substance place physical strain on joints and the cardiovascular system during routine movement, while the thick double coat that protected them in icy waters contributes to overheating in warmer conditions. Health robustness is challenged by the demands of their original water rescue and draft roles, requiring owners to manage weight carefully throughout the shorter lifespan.
answers.size: Newfoundlands reach 100-150 lb and stand 26-28 in at the shoulder. Their massive, heavily boned build with powerful shoulders and broad chest means even a gentle lean can knock over furniture or small children. Living with them involves navigating constant drool and the sensation of sharing space with a calm, bear-like presence that was bred for hauling heavy loads and performing water rescues.
answers.barking: Newfoundlands do not bark much. Their low tendency to vocalise stems from the quiet confidence developed during 17th- and 18th-century work alongside Canadian fishermen, where they focused on swimming rescues and pulling carts without unnecessary noise. The breed remains mostly silent unless a genuine need arises, offering a protective presence through sheer size rather than sound.
answers.apartment: No — Newfoundlands are poorly suited to apartment living. Their giant size and heavy build make them clumsy indoors, their thick double coat causes constant shedding and overheating in confined warm spaces, and their need for regular moderate exercise is hard to meet without access to cool water or open ground for their water-rescue heritage.
answers.first-time: No — Newfoundlands are not a good first dog because their high maintenance from giant size, heavy shedding and drooling demands constant commitment. The sheer scale of food bills, grooming needs and space requirements, combined with their protective loyalty that can lead to unintentional knocking over of objects, overwhelm most novices despite the breed’s gentle and patient temperament.
